title: How browser HTTP caching works
assumedKnowledge: You can read HTTP request and response headers.

concepts.title: Freshness and age
concepts.statement: Decide whether a stored response may be reused without contacting the origin, and work out how long it stays fresh.

options.text: Reuse the stored response without contacting the origin at all.
Send a conditional request and reuse the stored body only on a 304.
Fetch a complete new response, because the stored copy must not be served.

misconceptions.statement: A cache has to check with the origin before every reuse, even while the response is fresh.
Fresh means the origin has not changed the resource since the cache stored it.
A stale response is worthless and has to be thrown away and fetched again in full.
A stale response can keep being served exactly like a fresh one until the cache needs the space.

cards.heading: A fresh response can be reused
body: While a stored response is fresh, a cache may serve it to a matching request without contacting the origin at all. That is the whole point of freshness: it is a permission to reuse, granted in advance by the server, so the browser can answer from disk in a few milliseconds instead of waiting on a round trip.

Freshness is not a promise that the bytes are the newest ones on the origin. The server might have replaced the resource a second after it was stored. The cache has no way to know, and it is not expected to know. The origin accepted that risk when it declared a freshness lifetime with Cache-Control: max-age=60, which says: for 60 seconds, do not ask me.
So the question a cache asks is never has this changed? It is am I still allowed to reuse this? A fresh response answers yes.

cards.heading: Age measures stored time
body: A response's current age is the number of seconds it has spent stored, in any cache, since the origin generated it. The Age header carries that count downstream: a shared proxy that has held a response for 120 seconds forwards it with Age: 120, and the browser adds its own resident time on top.

Freshness ends when current age reaches the freshness lifetime. A response with max-age=300 that arrives already carrying Age: 120 has 180 seconds of freshness left, not 300, because the clock started at the origin rather than at the browser.

Once age passes the lifetime the response is stale. Stale does not mean useless. The cache keeps the bytes, and the usual next step is to ask the origin whether they are still good, which the next Concept covers. Discarding a stale response outright wastes a copy that is often still perfectly valid.

concepts.title: Validators and conditional requests
concepts.statement: Predict what a conditional request returns when the stored validator does or does not match the origin's current representation.

options.text: The origin answers 304 Not Modified and the cache keeps serving its stored body.
The origin answers 200 with a complete body and the cache replaces its stored copy.
The cache serves its stored body straight away without sending the origin anything.

misconceptions.statement: When the validator still matches, the origin resends the whole resource so the cache can be sure it is current.
Holding an ETag lets a cache reuse the response without any request, the same way freshness does.
The origin answers 304 whenever the cache holds any copy at all, whether or not the resource changed.

cards.heading: Validators name a version
body: A validator is a label for one exact version of a resource. ETag: "v7" is an opaque token the origin chooses; Last-Modified is a timestamp. Either one lets two parties agree on which bytes they are talking about without sending the bytes.

A validator is not a permission to reuse. Freshness answers may I serve this?; a validator answers which version is this? A cache that is holding a stale response with an ETag is still holding a stale response. What the ETag buys is a cheap way to find out whether that stale copy happens to be the current one.

That distinction drives the whole mechanism. When the origin's current representation carries the same ETag, the stored bytes are current. When the ETag differs, the resource changed and the stored copy is out of date, no matter how recently the cache fetched it.

cards.heading: Conditional requests avoid bodies
body: A stale cache revalidates by sending its validator back in a conditional request: If-None-Match: "v7". The origin compares that token with its current representation and answers with one of two responses.

If the token still matches, the origin sends 304 Not Modified with fresh headers and no body. The cache keeps the body it already has, updates the freshness information, and serves the stored bytes. For a 200 kilobyte image that means about 200 kilobytes stay off the wire and a few hundred bytes of headers travel instead.

If the token no longer matches, the origin sends an ordinary 200 OK with the complete new body, and the cache replaces its stored copy. Either way the cache learns the truth; the only difference is whether the bytes had to move.

concepts.title: Cache directives and revalidation
concepts.statement: Read a Cache-Control header and say what each directive requires of a cache before and after the response turns stale.

options.text: Do not keep any copy of the response in the cache, not even briefly.
Keep a copy and serve it without asking the origin for the stated seconds.
Keep a copy, but once stale never serve it without a successful check.

misconceptions.statement: no-store is a freshness hint, so the cache may still keep a copy for a while.
no-store means stored but immediately stale, ready to be revalidated before reuse.
must-revalidate forbids the cache from storing the response at all.
must-revalidate lets the cache keep serving the response without asking, as if it were still fresh.

cards.heading: Directives set the rules
body: Cache-Control is the origin telling caches how to behave, one directive at a time. max-age=600 declares a freshness lifetime: keep a copy and serve it without asking for 600 seconds, counted from when the origin generated the response. A response with max-age=600 that arrives carrying Age: 60 therefore has 540 seconds of freshness left.

no-store is a different kind of instruction. It does not shorten freshness to zero; it forbids storage. A cache must not write any part of the request or response to durable storage, and must not hold a copy to revalidate later. A page carrying a one-time payment confirmation is the classic case.
The difference matters because max-age=0 and no-store look similar and behave nothing alike. The first leaves a copy in place that a conditional request can rescue; the second leaves nothing.

cards.heading: must-revalidate limits stale reuse
body: By default a cache has some freedom with stale responses. If the origin cannot be reached, it may serve the stale copy rather than an error, and some configurations allow a little stale reuse while a revalidation runs in the background.

must-revalidate removes that freedom. The cache still stores the response and still serves it freely while fresh. Once the response is stale, though, the cache may serve it only after a successful revalidation with the origin. If the origin is down, the cache must return an error such as 504 Gateway Timeout instead of the stale bytes.

So max-age=600, must-revalidate reads as two rules in sequence: ten minutes of unquestioned reuse, then strict checking. It does not forbid storing and it does not extend freshness. Use it when serving an outdated version is worse than serving nothing, for instance an account balance.

questions.stem: A browser holds a stored response with Cache-Control: max-age=60 and a current age of 20 seconds. A matching request arrives. What may the cache do?

feedback.reuse: Correct. At 20 seconds of a 60-second lifetime the response is fresh, and freshness is permission to reuse without asking.
feedback.revalidate: Validation is for stale responses. This one is still fresh, so the origin told the cache not to ask yet.

questions.stem: A response arrives at a browser with Cache-Control: max-age=300 and Age: 120. For how many more seconds is it fresh?
questions.feedback: 180 seconds. Current age already stands at 120 of the 300-second lifetime, because the clock started at the origin.

questions.stem: Which response header carries the number of seconds a response has already spent in caches?
questions.feedback: Age. It counts seconds since the origin generated the response, and each cache passes it downstream.

questions.stem: A browser holds a stored response with Cache-Control: max-age=60, a current age of 90 seconds, and an ETag. A matching request arrives. What should the cache do?

feedback.revalidate: Correct. At 90 seconds the response is stale, so the cache asks the origin whether its copy is still good instead of serving it blindly.
feedback.reuse: The response is 30 seconds past its lifetime. Stale responses are not served as if fresh; they are checked first.
feedback.refetch: Stale is not worthless. The cache keeps the bytes and asks whether they are still valid, which is usually far cheaper than a full fetch.

questions.stem: A stale stored response carries ETag "v7". The browser sends If-None-Match: "v7" and the origin's current representation still has ETag "v7". What happens?

feedback.not_modified: Correct. A matching validator earns a 304 with no body, and the cache keeps serving the bytes it already holds.
feedback.full_response: A full 200 is what a changed resource gets. When the token matches there is nothing new to send, so the origin sends no body.
feedback.no_request: The response is stale, so the cache must ask. An ETag identifies a version; it does not grant reuse.

questions.stem: Which request header carries a stored ETag so the origin can compare it with its current representation?
questions.feedback: If-None-Match. The origin compares the token and answers 304 on a match or 200 with a new body otherwise.

questions.stem: A browser holds a stale 200 kilobyte image with an ETag. It revalidates with If-None-Match and the origin answers 304. About how many kilobytes of body does the browser avoid downloading?
questions.feedback: About 200 kilobytes. A 304 carries headers and no body, so the whole stored image stays where it is.

questions.stem: A stale stored response carries ETag "v7". The browser sends If-None-Match: "v7", but the origin's current representation now has ETag "v8". What happens?

feedback.full_response: Correct. The tokens differ, so the resource changed, and the origin sends a complete 200 for the cache to store in place of the old copy.
feedback.not_modified: 304 is only for a matching validator. "v7" and "v8" name different versions, so the stored copy is out of date.
feedback.no_request: The response is stale and must be checked. An ETag names a version; it never stands in for freshness.

questions.stem: A response arrives with Cache-Control: no-store. What does the directive require of a cache?

feedback.never_store: Correct. no-store forbids keeping any copy, so there is nothing to serve and nothing to revalidate later.
feedback.serve_for_lifetime: no-store says nothing about a lifetime. It is a ban on storage, not a short freshness window.
feedback.revalidate_when_stale: That describes max-age=0 or must-revalidate. With no-store there is no stored copy to check.

questions.stem: A response arrives with Cache-Control: max-age=600, must-revalidate. Eleven minutes later it is stale. What does must-revalidate require of the cache now?

feedback.revalidate_when_stale: Correct. Once stale, the response may be served only after a successful revalidation. If the origin is down, the cache returns an error instead.
feedback.never_store: must-revalidate does not forbid storing. The cache kept the copy and served it freely for ten minutes.
feedback.serve_for_lifetime: The lifetime ran out at 600 seconds. must-revalidate tightens what happens after that; it never extends freshness.

questions.stem: A response arrives at a browser with Cache-Control: max-age=600 and Age: 60. After how many more seconds does it become stale?
questions.feedback: 540 seconds. The 600-second lifetime is counted from the origin, and 60 of those seconds were spent upstream.

questions.stem: Which Cache-Control directive requires a stale response to pass a successful revalidation before a cache may serve it?
questions.feedback: must-revalidate. It leaves fresh reuse alone and forbids serving stale bytes without a successful check.
